name: Turquoise
lede: Turquoise is the blue-green of a copper-bearing stone whose French name points at Turkey, and the color has been worked into glaze, glass, smalt and printer's ink ever since.

sections.title: A stone and its name
sections.body:
Turquoise is the greenish blue of the gemstone of that name, and the word is usually explained as pointing to Turkey or Turkestan, which were regarded as the source of the stone [1]. Our library records the color word as first seen in 1573, in Maerz and Paul's dictionary [2].

On a color wheel it is a tertiary color: blue-green, sitting between blue and green [3]. Nineteenth-century wheel makers invented their own names for these in-between hues, and one scheme labelled its tertiaries sulphur, turquoise, garnet and nasturtium [4]. The names show how unstable color words were between the primaries.

Turquoise also marks a small might-have-been. Finlay points out that Newton chose indigo to make seven spectral bands, and could instead have named the turquoise that lies between green and blue [5]. The seven are Newton's choice, made for a tidy cosmological number, and not seven natural bands [5].

sections.title: Copper makes the color
sections.body:
The stone gets its color from copper: copper in the mineral produces the green and blue of [[gem:turquoise|turquoise]] [6]. Ball's chemical shorthand puts it this way. Iron is red, cobalt is deep blue, and copper claims the turquoise shade, which also appears as the greenish patina of aging copperwork [7]. Copper does the same in glass, where it turns a melt turquoise [8].

Persian potters used both metals on tiles. Finlay reports that cobalt gave the blue glaze and copper the turquoise, and he links the two to the heavens and to the green of the Prophet's cloak [9]. The symbolism is his reading and not a documented rule.

Werner's mineral system, as revised by Syme in 1821, matched the mineral turquoise to a swatch called Greenish Blue (no. 33), which Syme described as [[berlin-blue]] with white and a little emerald green [10]. That old plate is a reminder that a stone's name and a chart's [[greenish-blue]] were never the same thing [10].

sections.title: Mines, amulets and a very old thread
sections.body:
The ancient Egyptians worked turquoise mines at Serabit el-Khadem in the Sinai, and Finlay notes a shrine to Hathor underground there, a rare example of a miners' shrine [11]. Our library dates the color's earliest trace to roughly 1950 BC, and that figure is approximate [2]. Turquoise was valued but rare and expensive, which is one reason the Egyptians manufactured a blue instead [12].

That manufactured blue, [[egyptian-blue]], was first made around 2500 BC, and ground fine it came out as pale as turquoise, ground coarse as dark as [[lapis-lazuli]] [12]. Paterson lists Egyptian frit as an early turquoise-blue pigment [13].

Birren reports a Persian amulet custom: a turquoise set in the eye of a sacrificial lamb, the lamb roasted, and the stone sewn into a child's headdress [14]. Finlay's list of the stones on a biblical breastplate includes turquoise as one reading of a Hebrew name [15], but Pastoureau warns that identifying such stones with modern names is hard [16].

Among the oldest traces of linen ever found is a spun flax fibre from a cave in the Caucasus that had been dyed turquoise, about thirty thousand years ago [17].

sections.title: In the paint box
sections.body:
Pigment makers have long chased the shade with other recipes. Kunckel's 1689 book of recipes for goldsmiths includes a turquoise-coloured smalt, and a Venetian glassmaker's notebook of 1644 lists turquoise among its coloured smalts [18].

German writers made a pigment of the name. Turkish green and turquoise green are the same word there, and the pigment is a chromium aluminium cobalt oxide [19]. A color of that composition has been found in an 1862 painting by Schleich the Elder in Munich [19]. Cobalt turquoise, in English, is a blue made from cobalt titanium oxide [20], and the greener chromium version of [[cerulean-blue]] is often sold under the same name [21]. Manganese blue was also marketed as turquoise blue [22].

The great modern turquoise came from the laboratory. Monastral Fast Blue, a copper phthalocyanine with a deep turquoise hue, was developed by ICI between 1935 and 1937, and a green version made with chlorine followed in the 1950s [23]. Printers know a turquoise of their own: the sensitizer that reflects green and blue light is the one they call cyan [24].

An older word, venet, meant a turquoise blue and was short for the Latin for Venice blue [25]. Maerz and Paul link it to sails painted that color on spy ships in the fifteenth century, for camouflage [25]. Pastoureau reads the Roman chariot-racing faction called the veneti as a vivid turquoise, though he admits that without a comparison no answer is possible [26].

sections.title: Words, jealousy and mourning
sections.body:
A popular Renaissance guide to color symbolism, quoted by Greenfield, called turquoise a sure sign of jealousy [27]. In Central Asia turquoise blue has been a common mourning color [28]. The Aztec name for the indigo plant, xiuhquilitl, is built from the words for turquoise and vegetable [29].

Modern English attached the word to many things [30]. Duck-egg blue is a light turquoise, Tiffany blue is the turquoise of a jeweller, and Chinese three-colour ware used aubergine, blue and turquoise [30]. The nearest named neighbors are [[tiffany-blue]], [[robin-s-egg-blue]], [[medium-turquoise]] and [[teal]] [2]. Turquoise is also a December birthstone in the traditional lists, shared with blue [[gem:topaz|topaz]] [30].

Linguists disagree on its status. Batchelor, listing the common terms, treats turquoise as a specialized word, less basic than the Berlin-Kay terms [31]. A 2015 online naming study by Mylonas and MacDonald argued that turquoise and lilac should count as basic English color terms, a position that remains contested [32]. Birren's old opinion that turquoise in a kitchen shortens the apparent passage of time is not evidence [38].

sections.title: The color of the universe
sections.body:
In January 2002 a team at Johns Hopkins University announced that the averaged light of some 200,000 galaxies was pale turquoise [33]. Three months later they issued an embarrassed correction. A computer bug was to blame, and the true average was beige [33]. The turquoise-universe story is a myth in the form usually repeated.

Books disagree about it. Paterson's dictionary entry repeats the first announcement, saying the average comes out a few per cent greener than turquoise, with no correction [1]. Finlay, who reports the retraction, is the safer source [33].

sections.title: The swatch and the eye
sections.body:
The swatch on this page is the CSS color `turquoise`, #40E0D0, a bright, light blue-green [2]. The nearest ISCC-NBS block is "brilliant bluish green", about 5 CIEDE2000 units away, and the 2010 XKCD survey's turquoise (#06C2AC) is darker and greener [2]. None of these is the pale blue-green of a worn stone, which Werner matched to a different swatch [10].

To see how unstable the color is, look at what surrounds it. Eckstut shows that a turquoise square looks bluer on a green ground and greener on a blue one [34]. Put the same turquoise beside a gem or a swimming pool and compare: the Paraiba tourmaline, which is heat-treated, is described as the intense turquoise of swimming pools and sold for about $40,000 a carat [37].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 museum paintings, as photographed, none has this exact turquoise (within CIEDE2000 4) over at least 1 per cent of its canvas [35]. The archive holds aged, varnished paintings, so the gap describes this archive and says nothing about painting as a whole [35].

In printed English, turquoise used as an adjective stood at about two thirds of its 2010 peak by 2000, and it rose fastest after 2000 [36]. It is a modern word by volume, though an old one by name [36].
